slides.heading: Junior AI Navigators
slides.narration: Welcome back to Ground School with Captain Naomi. [warmly] This is Junior AI Navigators, Week 6: AI Storytelling. Today you get to be an author, so grab your imagination. You'll need it.

slides.heading: Pre-Flight
slides.narration: Here's your Pre-Flight. Today, your imagination leads the adventure. First you'll explore, using AI to brainstorm short story ideas. Then you'll create. You choose, change, write and draw your very own story. And your mission? Make an eight-page mini book, and say who helped.

slides.heading: Take-Off Question
slides.narration: Time for our Take-Off Question. What if you copy a whole story that AI wrote? Think about it. Who chose the words, the characters and the ending? [short pause] Now it's your turn. How could you take a more active role as the author? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: You stay the author
slides.narration: You stay the author. That means you make the creative decisions. AI can suggest things, like a starting idea, a possible problem or a useful word. But you decide what belongs in your story and what to leave out. And you create it, writing your own sentences and drawing your own pictures.

slides.heading: Your storytelling flight plan
slides.narration: Here's your storytelling flight plan, in three steps. Ask: request some short ideas. Choose: pick one, mix them, or say no thanks. Create: write and draw your story. Ask, choose, create. Let's fly through them one at a time.

slides.heading: Step 1: Ask for ideas
slides.narration: Step one: ask for ideas. Keep your request short and clear. Start with your character. Ours is a wombat who wants to fly. Then your request: three different ideas. And your format: just one sentence for each idea. Short and clear, like a good radio call.

slides.heading: A prompt to try
slides.narration: Here's a prompt to try, with your grown-up doing the typing. [short pause] "Give me three different ideas for a story about a wombat who wants to fly. Just one sentence each." [short pause] Remember, you ask for ideas, and then you make the choices yourself.

slides.heading: Remember WHAT, WHO and HOW
slides.narration: Remember WHAT, WHO and HOW? They help you tell the idea crew what you need. WHAT do you want? Three different story ideas about a flying wombat. WHO is it for? A reader aged eight to eleven. And HOW should the answer look? One sentence for each idea.

slides.heading: Three possible starting points
slides.narration: Here are three possible starting points. Paper Wings: a wombat tests wings made from fallen leaves. Balloon Basket: a wombat builds a balloon to visit the clouds. Bird Ride: a wombat asks a giant bird for a lift. [laughs softly] Three very different ways to get one wombat off the ground.

slides.heading: Step 2: YOU choose
slides.narration: Step two belongs to you. You choose, and you can say yes, mix or no. Pick one, the idea that sparks your imagination. Mix two, combining parts into a different adventure. Or reject them all. Yes, that's allowed! You may already have a better idea.

slides.heading: Your choice has a reason
slides.narration: Your choice has a reason. So ask yourself, what makes you want to tell this story? Maybe it's a character, someone you want to follow. Maybe it's a problem, something interesting to solve. Or maybe it's a possibility, an ending you want to discover.

slides.heading: Step 3: YOU write and draw
slides.narration: Step three: you write and draw. This is where a starting point turns into a real story. Your words: write the sentences yourself. Your pictures: show the adventure in your own drawing style. And your pace: no rushing. You can work on it over several sessions.

slides.heading: Small requests can help
slides.narration: Stuck? Small requests can help, so ask for just a little help. For a problem idea, you might ask, "What could go wrong for my wombat?" For a word idea, try, "Give me a word that means really, really big." Then use your judgement. Read the suggestion and decide whether it fits your story.

slides.heading: The Three Changes Rule
slides.narration: Now for the Three Changes Rule. Character: change a name, or something special that makes them different. Setting: move the adventure somewhere new. Ending: choose a different way to solve the problem.

slides.heading: Make three meaningful changes
slides.narration: Make three meaningful changes, so the idea grows in your own direction. That means more than swapping words. Change details that affect what happens. You could also add a funny mistake, a new helper or a surprise. And keep track. Write down the three changes you made.

slides.heading: An example of three changes
slides.narration: Let's try one together. The starting idea: a wombat builds a balloon to visit the clouds. Change one, the character: Pip is a wombat who is afraid of heights. [laughs softly] Change two, the setting: the adventure starts at a windy beach. Change three, the ending: Pip builds a kite and stays safely on the sand.

slides.heading: Instrument Check
slides.narration: Instrument Check! In this activity, who is the author? Think about it. Who chooses, who writes and who draws? Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Instrument Check: answer
slides.narration: [warmly] You are! AI is the idea crew. The helper offers starting points and suggestions. The author makes the decisions and creates the story, and that's you. And the illustrator? That's you too.

slides.heading: Why draw the pictures yourself?
slides.narration: Why draw the pictures yourself? Because nobody draws exactly like you. Show your imagination by choosing the colours, the expressions and the little details. Try your own style. Stick figures, patterns and simple shapes all count. For this mission, use pencils and paper for your illustrations.

slides.heading: Be honest about help
slides.narration: Be honest about help, and tell your reader who helped make your book. If AI helped with ideas, say so at the end of your story. There's a special line you can use, and it fits when you wrote the story and drew the pictures yourself. If you had other help, describe that help honestly too.

slides.heading: Your honesty line
slides.narration: Here is your honesty line. [short pause] "Ideas helped by AI. Story and pictures by me." Put this on the last page, but only if it's true about how you made your book. Good creators acknowledge help. That means they say who helped them.

slides.heading: Mission: My Mini Book
slides.narration: Mission time: My Mini Book! First, gather your author's kit. Paper: two sheets, folded together. Drawing tools: coloured pencils or crayons. And your co-pilot: a grown-up to help with the tool and with binding your book.

slides.heading: Build an eight-page book
slides.narration: Let's build an eight-page book. Lay one sheet on top of the other, fold them in half together, and press a good crease along the middle. Next, bind the fold. Ask a grown-up to staple it, or to help you tie it with string. Now count the surfaces. You have eight pages, including the front and the back.

slides.heading: Plan your eight pages
slides.narration: Plan your eight pages. Page one is the cover, with a title, a picture and your author name. Pages two and three are the beginning: meet the character and discover their goal. Pages four and five, the middle: a problem appears, and the character tries something. Pages six and seven show what changes and how it ends. Page eight is thanks and help: your honesty line and a final drawing.

slides.heading: Your mission checklist
slides.narration: Here's your mission checklist. Choose. Change. Write. Draw. First, with your grown-up, ask for three short ideas and choose one. Next, make at least three creative changes. Then write, illustrate, and add your honesty line.

slides.heading: No chatbot? Try story dice
slides.narration: No chatbot? No problem. Try story dice instead, and make an idea list with your grown-up. Roll one is your character, for example a wombat, a kookaburra or a sleepy dragon. Roll two is the place, like a beach, the moon or a treehouse. Roll three is the problem, maybe a lost map or a missing birthday cake.

slides.heading: Your story dice lists
slides.narration: Here are your story dice lists. Your character could be a wombat, kookaburra, dragon, koala, octopus or explorer. The place could be a beach, the moon, a treehouse, a garden, a castle, or under the sea. And the problem? A lost map, a missing cake, a broken bridge, a sudden storm, mixed-up parcels, or a very loud noise. Roll once for each list, then invent your adventure.

slides.heading: Welcome back, authors
slides.narration: Welcome back, authors! [warmly] Tell us about your adventure. Who is your character? What are they called, and what do they want? Which three changes did you make? And show us your favourite part, a sentence or a picture you created. Pause the video and share it with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Oops! Moment
slides.narration: Oops! Moment. A whole AI story may miss your idea. The problem is that copying without reading leaves you with choices you didn't want. A better request is to ask for short ideas you can review. And remember Week 5. Even clear instructions do not guarantee a good or true answer.

slides.heading: Remember Rhyme
slides.narration: Here's our Remember Rhyme. Say it with me. [short pause] AI gives ideas. I make it mine. You make the choices, the words and the pictures. Then remember to tell your reader if AI helped with ideas. One more time. AI gives ideas. I make it mine.

slides.heading: Quick Check 1
slides.narration: Quick Check one. What is the Three Changes Rule? Your turn: name three things you could change. Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 1: answer
slides.narration: How did you go? The rule is to change at least three things. For example, the character's name, the setting and the ending. Your purpose is to develop the starting idea with your own decisions.

slides.heading: Quick Check 2
slides.narration: Quick Check two. What do honest authors write at the end? Your turn. Think about who helped with the ideas. Pause the video and talk it over with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 2: answer
slides.narration: Honest authors say who helped. For this mission, that's your honesty line: "Ideas helped by AI. Story and pictures by me." And always describe the help accurately.

slides.heading: Quick Check 3
slides.narration: Quick Check three. Can you finish last week's rhyme from Week 5? It starts, "Sounds sure..." [short pause] What comes next? Pause the video and say it with your grown-up. [pause]

slides.heading: Quick Check 3: answer
slides.narration: Sounds sure, check for sure! [warmly] That's the Captain's Check. Does it make sense? Check elsewhere. Ask a grown-up. And for stories, if you include any factual details, check those too.

slides.heading: Your Flight Log
slides.narration: Time for your Flight Log. What came from your imagination? Record your story title and your three changes. Reflect: which sentence, picture or joke came only from you? And notice: how did you use a suggestion without copying the whole story? Pause the video and fill in your Flight Log. [pause]

slides.heading: Grown-Up Corner
slides.narration: Now a quick word for the grown-ups. Please support the storyteller's decisions. Help with access: use a suitable tool under its rules, and keep personal details out. Encourage their voice. Let the learner choose, write and draw, and spelling can wait. Review suggestions together, reject unsuitable material, and take breaks as needed.

slides.heading: Author
slides.narration: [warmly] You've earned your Week 6 Flight Log stamp: Author! You explored AI as a source of starting ideas. You created your own words, your own pictures and your own creative changes. Next week, it's Scratch Helpers: rules we write, and learning from examples. See you then, authors.
